transcript.speaker: S1
transcript.text: Hello and welcome to Culture Matters. This week, we're asking whether public libraries still have a place in the digital age. Many people assume that libraries are dying, because you can download a book or find an answer in seconds on your phone. But the evidence from my research is more complicated.

transcript.speaker: S1
transcript.text: First, the figures. In the past decade, the number of books borrowed in the UK has fallen by about a third. That's the statistic politicians like to quote when they want to cut library budgets. And it's true that more than seven hundred libraries have closed since 2010. However, the number of people actually visiting libraries has not fallen nearly as much. In many places, visits are the same or even higher. So what are people doing there, if they aren't borrowing as many books?

transcript.speaker: S1
transcript.text: I visited a library in Leeds last month to find out. In the morning, it was full of parents with toddlers attending a story session. Around lunchtime, older people were learning to use tablets in a free class. By the afternoon, school students had taken over the quiet room to do their homework. And I spoke to a man in his forties who was using the computers to apply for jobs, because he doesn't have internet at home. About one in ten households in the UK still doesn't have a reliable connection, and for them the library is essential.

transcript.speaker: S1
transcript.text: Librarians told me their role has changed. They are no longer simply people who stamp books. They help with forms, run language classes and sometimes act as a first point of contact for people with problems they don't know how to solve. One librarian called it social care in disguise, which I found a striking phrase.

transcript.speaker: S1
transcript.text: Not everyone is convinced. A critic I interviewed argued that libraries try to do too much, and that other organisations should provide these services. She thinks that money would be better spent on schools. But when I put that to the librarian, she answered that schools aren't open on Saturdays, and libraries are.

transcript.speaker: S1
transcript.text: Some libraries are experimenting with new ideas. In Helsinki, a modern central library offers 3D printers, sewing machines and a recording studio. Members can borrow these in the same way as books. It was designed with citizens' input, and it attracts over three million visitors a year.

transcript.speaker: S1
transcript.text: So, are libraries dying? My conclusion is no, but they're certainly changing. The challenge is whether funding will change with them. After the break, I'll be speaking to a council leader who has to decide the budget. Stay with us.
